title: 1-D DP: House Robber
oneLiner: Pick values from a row to maximize the total, never taking two neighbors -- decided one house at a time with two numbers.
keyTakeaway: At each house there are only two choices: skip it (keep the best total up to the previous house) or rob it (its value plus the best total up to two houses back). best[i] = max(best[i-1], best[i-2] + nums[i]), and since only the last two answers are ever read, two rolling variables replace the array.
explanation:
A row of houses holds nums[i] money each. Robbing two adjacent houses sets off an alarm, so you can't pick neighbors. What's the most you can collect? For [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] the answer is 12 (2 + 9 + 1).

Greedy shortcuts fail. "Take every other house" misses [2, 1, 1, 2], where the best is 2 + 2 = 4 using houses 0 and 3, which are three apart. "Always take the biggest remaining" fails on [5, 6, 5], where taking 6 blocks both 5s. You need to consider both options at every house, and DP does that without trying all 2^n subsets.

Define best[i] as the most money from houses 0 through i. For house i, either you skip it, and the answer is best[i-1], or you rob it, so house i-1 is off limits and the answer is nums[i] + best[i-2]. Take the larger. With best[-1] = best[-2] = 0 the formula also covers the first two houses. Notice that each step reads only the previous two answers, so keep two variables: prev2 (best two houses back) and prev1 (best up to the previous house). Each house computes cur = max(prev1, prev2 + nums[i]), then shifts: prev2 = prev1, prev1 = cur. That's O(n) time and O(1) space.

This "take it or skip it, and taking it rules out the neighbor" recurrence is the template for a family of problems. Common follow-ups: the houses are in a CIRCLE (house 0 and house n-1 are neighbors, so run the linear version twice, once without the first house and once without the last, and take the max), the houses form a binary tree (each node returns a pair: best if robbed, best if not), or "delete and earn", which turns into house robber after bucketing values.

The visualization walks [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]. The highlighted house is being decided; the tracker shows prev1, the best total so far.

recognitionSignals: Choose a subset of items in a line to maximize a sum, where choosing one item forbids its immediate neighbor(s).
Each position has a small, fixed set of choices (take or skip), and the best answer for a prefix depends only on the last one or two prefixes.
gotchas: Empty input returns 0 and a single house returns its own value -- seed prev1 = prev2 = 0 and the loop handles both.
Shift the variables in the right order: compute cur first, then prev2 = prev1, then prev1 = cur. Overwriting prev1 before reading it loses the skip option.
"Every other house" (sum of even indices vs. odd indices) is not the answer; the best picks can be more than one house apart.
confusableWith: Dynamic Programming: Climbing Stairs (Fundamentals) has the same two-variable rolling shape, but adds the previous two answers (counting ways) instead of taking a max over a choice.
0/1 Knapsack (this track) is also take-or-skip per item, but the constraint is a weight budget, so it needs a second dimension. Here the only constraint is adjacency, so one dimension is enough.

complexity.note: One pass over the houses; each step reads only the previous two answers, so two rolling variables replace the dp array (keeping the full array is O(n) space).
